generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, this is where many projects are won or lost, whatever the subject. A proposal that names a clear question, says why it matters, and sets out how the work will be done gives the project something to steer by. Working through those questions is what turns a broad interest, say in a topic you care about, into a study with limits you can actually meet.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students are interested in the same broad area, and each writes a short proposal.

Student A writes that the area is interesting and important, lists several things that could be looked at, and promises to read widely and report back. The proposal is eager, but it sets no focused question and no plan. With nothing to guide it, the project could go anywhere, and Student A will struggle to know when it is finished.

Student B works through a series of questions: what exactly do I want to find out, what is already known, what fresh angle am I taking, and how will I go about it? Each answer narrows the project to one question, with a clear plan and clear limits. The proposal has become a framework.

Both students began with the same interest. Only Student B used guiding questions to shape it into a study that can actually be run.
generatedProse.summary: A research proposal shapes a project: it turns a broad interest into a focused study with a plan you can carry out. Built from a series of guiding questions, it becomes a framework for the whole project. You can now explain what a proposal is for, and recognise how guiding questions do the shaping. The next lesson looks at the shape a project takes on the page.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Student B do that turned a broad interest into a workable study?

items.text: Student B worked through guiding questions that narrowed the interest to one question with a clear plan.
Student B promised to read widely and report back on the whole area.
Student B listed several things about the area that could be looked at.
Student B chose a topic that was more interesting than Student A's.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B used guiding questions to narrow the interest into one question with a clear plan.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that narrowed the interest and set a plan, rather than widening it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B worked through guiding questions that narrowed the interest to one question with a clear plan. Reading widely or listing possibilities leaves the project unshaped.

The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
